The identification of conceptual spaces and how they arise from accuracy-compression tradeoffs is underexplored.
future_direction: Combining different methods for robustness analysis to increase reliability in concept identification.
Using synthetic datasets with labeled intermediate concepts to test and improve methods for identifying concepts.
Developing methods to understand how entire conceptual spaces are formed holistically in DNNs.
papers.abstract: The present paper reviews and discusses work from computer science that proposes to identify concepts in internal representations (hidden layers) of DNNs. It is examined, first, how existing methods actually identify concepts that are supposedly represented in DNNs. Second, it is discussed how conceptual spaces -- sets of concepts in internal representations -- are shaped by a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression. These issues are critically examined by drawing on philosophy. While there is evidence that DNNs able to represent non-trivial inferential relations between concepts, our ability to identify concepts is severely limited.

papers.title: Emergent Visual-Semantic Hierarchies in Image-Text Representations
papers.research_question: Do vision-language foundation models exhibit emergent understanding of visual-semantic hierarchies, and how can we probe and enhance this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Foundation vision-language models exhibit emergent hierarchical understanding, and the proposed Radial Embedding framework can probe and enhance this understanding via text-only fine-tuning while retaining pretraining knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Foundation VLMs possess emergent hierarchical knowledge, and the RE framework can reveal and enhance this knowledge, enabling better hierarchical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation VLMs show zero-shot hierarchical understanding, outperforming prior models designed for hierarchy.
The Radial Embedding framework effectively probes hierarchical geometry in VLM embeddings.
Fine-tuning with RE loss improves hierarchical understanding without forgetting pretraining knowledge.
The HierarCaps dataset serves as a benchmark for hierarchical multimodal understanding.
papers.limitation: The automatically generated HierarCaps dataset may contain noise due to limitations of the language model and text-only pipeline.
papers.abstract: While recent vision-and-language models (VLMs) like CLIP are a powerful tool for analyzing text and images in a shared semantic space, they do not explicitly model the hierarchical nature of the set of texts which may describe an image. Conversely, existing multimodal hierarchical representation learning methods require costly training from scratch, failing to leverage the knowledge encoded by state-of-the-art multimodal foundation models. In this work, we study the knowledge of existing foundation models, finding that they exhibit emergent understanding of visual-semantic hierarchies despite not being directly trained for this purpose. We propose the Radial Embedding (RE) framework for probing and optimizing hierarchical understanding, and contribute the HierarCaps dataset, a benchmark facilitating the study of hierarchical knowledge in image--text representations, constructed automatically via large language models. Our results show that foundation VLMs exhibit zero-shot hierarchical understanding, surpassing the performance of prior models explicitly designed for this purpose. Furthermore, we show that foundation models may be better aligned to hierarchical reasoning via a text-only fine-tuning phase, while retaining pretraining knowledge.

papers.title: Exploring the Role of BERT Token Representations to Explain Sentence Probing Results
papers.research_question: What role do specific token representations play in BERT's ability to encode linguistic features and explain probing results?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes linguistic features in specific token representations, and gradient-based attribution can reveal these subspaces to explain probing performance.
papers.conclusion: BERT's token representations encode specific linguistic knowledge, and attribution methods provide insights into probing results, revealing distinct subspaces for different features.
papers.key_findings:
Sentence-ending tokens retain positional information in higher layers.
The ##s token encodes both noun number and verb tense information, and BERT separates these usages into distinct subspaces.
In bi-gram shift tasks, inverted tokens have higher attribution scores, and abnormalities are encoded in their representations.
In coordination inversion, coordinators like 'and' and 'but' play a key role, and their representations change significantly.
Attribution patterns are consistent even with less training data, indicating that knowledge is well-encoded in representations.
future_direction: Investigate how subspaces evolve during fine-tuning
Check if behaviors are affected by different training objectives
Use token-level analysis for model efficiency
papers.abstract: Several studies have been carried out on revealing linguistic features captured by BERT. This is usually achieved by training a diagnostic classifier on the representations obtained from different layers of BERT. The subsequent classification accuracy is then interpreted as the ability of the model in encoding the corresponding linguistic property. Despite providing insights, these studies have left out the potential role of token representations. In this paper, we provide a more in-depth analysis on the representation space of BERT in search for distinct and meaningful subspaces that can explain the reasons behind these probing results. Based on a set of probing tasks and with the help of attribution methods we show that BERT tends to encode meaningful knowledge in specific token representations (which are often ignored in standard classification setups), allowing the model to detect syntactic and semantic abnormalities, and to distinctively separate grammatical number and tense subspaces. 1

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Information Structure in Mappings: An Approach to Learning, Representation, and Generalisation
papers.research_question: How can we describe the structure of representations in neural networks, how does this structure emerge during training, and what kinds of structures enable generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis introduces quantitative methods for identifying systematic structure in mappings between spaces, and leverages them to understand how deep-learning models learn to represent information, what representational structures drive generalisation, and how design decisions condition the structures that emerge. It also introduces a novel, performant approach to estimating the entropy of vector space.
papers.conclusion: The thesis concludes that information structure methods provide insights into how models learn and generalize, drawing parallels between neural networks and human language.
papers.key_findings:
The methods can identify systematic structure in mappings and relate it to generalization.
There are distinct phases of training: early learning of lexical information followed by contextualization.
Model size affects representational structure: larger models develop more robust representations.
Information structure measures can predict downstream performance.
Regularity in representations is important for generalization.
papers.limitation: It’s unclear if the learnability of a language at timestep n matters at n+1 when the language has changed.
future_direction: Further study of the role learnability plays in an emergent context, where what is learned changes, is needed to understand the full picture.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable success of large large-scale neural networks, we still lack unified notation for thinking about and describing their representational spaces. We lack methods to reliably describe how their representations are structured, how that structure emerges over training, and what kinds of structures are desirable. This thesis introduces quantitative methods for identifying systematic structure in a mapping between spaces, and leverages them to understand how deep-learning models learn to represent information, what representational structures drive generalisation, and how design decisions condition the structures that emerge. To do this I identify structural primitives present in a mapping, along with information theoretic quantifications of each. These allow us to analyse learning, structure, and generalisation across multi-agent reinforcement learning models, sequence-to-sequence models trained on a single task, and Large Language Models. I also introduce a novel, performant, approach to estimating the entropy of vector space, that allows this analysis to be applied to models ranging in size from 1 million to 12 billion parameters. The experiments here work to shed light on how large-scale distributed models of cognition learn, while allowing us to draw parallels between those systems and their human analogs. They show how the structures of language and the constraints that give rise to them in many ways parallel the kinds of structures that drive performance of contemporary neural networks.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: A Survey on Mechanistic Interpretability for Multi-Modal Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can LLM interpretability methods be adapted to multimodal foundation models, and what are the mechanistic differences between unimodal and multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability for multimodal foundation models, introducing a taxonomy and comparing insights between unimodal and multimodal models to highlight research gaps.
papers.conclusion: The survey reviews mechanistic understanding methods for MMFMs, introduces a taxonomy differentiating interpretability methods adapted from language models and those designed for multimodal models, and compares mechanistic insights to identify gaps and their impact on downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
LLM-based interpretability methods can be extended to MMFMs with moderate adjustments, particularly when treating visual and textual inputs similarly.
Novel multimodal challenges arise such as interpreting visual embeddings in human-understandable terms, necessitating new dedicated analysis methods.
While interpretability aids downstream tasks, applications like hallucination mitigation and model editing remain underdeveloped in multimodal models compared to language models.
There is a substantial gap between the interpretability of LLMs and MMFMs, with a lack of unified benchmarks and tools for multimodal interpretability.
The survey proposes a three-dimensional taxonomy for mechanistic interpretability in multimodal models based on model family, interpretability techniques, and applications.
papers.limitation:
The survey mainly focuses on image-text multimodal models without considering other modalities such as video, time series, or 3D.
The survey does not contain experimental analysis because of the lack of unified benchmarks.
The survey only focuses on transformer-based or diffusion models, without considering novel model architectures such as MAMBA.
future_direction: Extending mechanistic interpretability techniques to analyze unified vision-text understanding and generation models.
Developing sequential batch model editing techniques for multimodal models, including diffusion and multimodal language models.
Exploring the effectiveness of sparse autoencoders and their variants for controlling and steering multimodal models.
papers.abstract: The rise of foundation models has transformed machine learning research, prompting efforts to uncover their inner workings and develop more efficient and reliable applications for better control. While significant progress has been made in interpreting Large Language Models (LLMs), multimodal foundation models (MMFMs) - such as contrastive vision-language models, generative vision-language models, and text-to-image models - pose unique interpretability challenges beyond unimodal frameworks. Despite initial studies, a substantial gap remains between the interpretability of LLMs and MMFMs. This survey explores two key aspects: (1) the adaptation of LLM interpretability methods to multimodal models and (2) understanding the mechanistic differences between unimodal language models and crossmodal systems. By systematically reviewing current MMFM analysis techniques, we propose a structured taxonomy of interpretability methods, compare insights across unimodal and multimodal architectures, and highlight critical research gaps.

papers.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the final layer always yield the best representation for downstream tasks, or can intermediate layers provide better representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intermediate layers in language models often outperform final layers on downstream tasks, and introduces a unified information-theoretic framework to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that intermediate layers often provide superior representations, challenging the default use of final layers, and provides a framework for understanding representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers across diverse architectures and tasks.
Autoregressive models exhibit a pronounced mid-layer compression valley, while masked or bidirectional models show milder changes.
The effect is domain-general, also observed in autoregressive vision transformers.
Chain-of-thought fine-tuning reshapes mid-layer entropy, preserving latent context for multi-step reasoning.
Intermediate layers strike a balance between information compression and signal preservation.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying causes of intermediate layer compression and do explicit finetuning to control compression.
papers.abstract: From extracting features to generating text, the outputs of large language models (LLMs) typically rely on the final layers, following the conventional wisdom that earlier layers capture only low-level cues. However, our analysis shows that intermediate layers can encode even richer representations, often improving performance on a range of downstream tasks. To explain and quantify these hidden-layer properties, we propose a unified framework of representation quality metrics based on information theory, geometry, and invariance to input perturbations. Our framework highlights how each layer balances information compression and signal preservation, revealing why mid-depth embeddings can exceed the last layer's performance. Through extensive experiments on 32 text-embedding tasks across various architectures (transformers, state-space models) and domains (language, vision), we demonstrate that intermediate layers consistently provide stronger features, challenging the standard view on final-layer embeddings and opening new directions on using mid-layer representations for more robust and accurate representations.

papers.title: How Does Selective Mechanism Improve Self-Attention Networks?
papers.research_question: How does the selective mechanism improve self-attention networks (SANs)? Specifically, what are the underlying reasons for the strong performance of selective SANs?
papers.core_contribution: The selective mechanism, implemented via Gumbel-Softmax, improves self-attention networks by mitigating their weaknesses in word order encoding and syntactic structure modeling, primarily by focusing attention on semantically important content words.
papers.conclusion: The selective mechanism mitigates two major weaknesses of self-attention networks—word order encoding and structure modeling—by enabling the model to focus on content words, which is essential for natural language understanding and generation.
papers.key_findings:
SSANs consistently outperform standard SANs on multiple NLP tasks (natural language inference, semantic role labeling, machine translation).
SSANs improve the ability to capture both local and global word order information, as shown by higher accuracy on word reordering detection tasks.
SSANs produce more syntactic representations and better model sentence structure, as evidenced by improved performance on linguistic probing tasks (TreeDepth, TopConst).
The selective mechanism helps SANs by paying more attention to content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and less to function words (prepositions, determiners, punctuation).
Applying the selective mechanism to the first encoder layer yields the most significant improvements for word order tasks, suggesting lexical information is crucial.
papers.limitation: The findings are validated on specific SAN architectures and tasks; their generalizability to other architectures (e.g., BERT) and more general attention models remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validating the findings on other SAN architectures (e.g., BERT).
Extending the analysis to more general attention models.
papers.abstract: Self-attention networks (SANs) with selective mechanism has produced substantial improvements in various NLP tasks by concentrating on a subset of input words. However, the underlying reasons for their strong performance have not been well explained. In this paper, we bridge the gap by assessing the strengths of selective SANs (SSANs), which are implemented with a flexible and universal Gumbel-Softmax. Experimental results on several representative NLP tasks, including natural language inference, semantic role labelling, and machine translation, show that SSANs consistently outperform the standard SANs. Through well-designed probing experiments, we empirically validate that the improvement of SSANs can be attributed in part to mitigating two commonly-cited weaknesses of SANs: word order encoding and structure modeling. Specifically, the selective mechanism improves SANs by paying more attention to content words that contribute to the meaning of the sentence. The code and data are released at https://github.com/xwgeng/SSAN.

papers.title: Language Through a Prism: A Spectral Approach for Multiscale Language\n Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do deep models capture information at different scales (from subwords to documents), and can we force them to better capture structure across this hierarchy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a spectral filtering framework to disentangle scale-specific information in language model representations and a prism layer that trains models to specialize neurons for different scales, improving performance on long-range tasks.
papers.conclusion: Spectral techniques are a powerful set of tools for uncovering and modeling multiscale phenomena in deep NLP models.
papers.key_findings:
Spectral filters can disentangle scale-specific information in BERT representations, with high-pass filters useful for word-level tasks and low-pass filters for document-level tasks.
The prism layer enables BERT to produce multiscale representations that improve performance on utterance- and document-level tasks while maintaining word-level performance.
Training with the prism layer increases the model's sensitivity to long-range context in masked language modeling.
The method is general and could be applied to other domains like images, audio, and video.
future_direction: Applying the spectral techniques to other domains such as computer vision, time series, and reinforcement learning models.
Using the tools for interpretability research to better understand knowledge and information processing at different scales.
Applying the method to track topics over time in linguistic change research.
papers.abstract:
Language exhibits structure at different scales, ranging from subwords to
words, sentences, paragraphs, and documents. To what extent do deep models
capture information at these scales, and can we force them to better capture
structure across this hierarchy? We approach this question by focusing on
individual neurons, analyzing the behavior of their activations at different
timescales. We show that signal processing provides a natural framework for
separating structure across scales, enabling us to 1) disentangle
scale-specific information in existing embeddings and 2) train models to learn
more about particular scales. Concretely, we apply spectral filters to the
activations of a neuron across an input, producing filtered embeddings that
perform well on part of speech tagging (word-level), dialog speech acts
classification (utterance-level), or topic classification (document-level),
while performing poorly on the other tasks. We also present a prism layer for
training models, which uses spectral filters to constrain different neurons to
model structure at different scales. Our proposed BERT + Prism model can better
predict masked tokens using long-range context and produces multiscale
representations that perform better at utterance- and document-level tasks. Our
methods are general and readily applicable to other domains besides language,
such as images, audio, and video.

papers.title: Neural dynamic foundations of a theory of higher cognition: the case of grounding nested phrases
papers.research_question: How can higher cognitive competences (productivity, systematicity, compositionality) emerge from grounded sensory-motor processes? Specifically, how can nested relational and action phrases be represented and perceptually grounded in a neural dynamic architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a neural dynamic architecture based on Dynamic Field Theory (DFT) that represents and perceptually grounds nested relational and action phrases, demonstrating how productivity, systematicity, and compositionality can emerge from grounded sensory-motor processes.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic Field Theory provides a neural process account for higher cognition that is grounded in perception and action, capable of handling the productivity, systematicity, and compositionality observed in language and thought.
papers.key_findings:
The architecture represents nested phrases by binding localist neural representations through a shared index dimension, enabling flexible expression of interdependencies among components.
Sequences of neural processing steps are autonomously generated to attentionally select referenced objects and events in a manner sensitive to their interdependencies.
The model solves the problem of grounding complex nested phrases, such as 'the small tree that is to the left of the lake which is to the left of the large tree'.
The work extends earlier DFT models by incorporating new types of grammatical constructions and a larger vocabulary.
The architecture demonstrates how coordinate transforms (via neural gain fields) enable the application of neural circuitry across different inputs, emulating the generality of function calls in symbolic computation.
papers.limitation:
The model currently handles a limited set of grammatical constructions and vocabulary.
The extensive neural connectivity required to link hundreds of thousands of concepts into the conceptual structure may be a bottleneck, potentially requiring multiple instances organized by semantic domains.
future_direction: Extending the model to handle more complex grammatical structures and a larger set of concepts.
Incorporating learning mechanisms to understand how the patterned connectivity giving nodes their sensory-motor meaning arises from experience.
Exploring how multiple instances of conceptual structure representations, organized by semantic domains, might handle dependencies among semantically remote items.
papers.abstract: Because cognitive competences emerge in evolution and development from the sensory-motor domain, we seek a neural process account for higher cognition in which all representations are necessarily grounded in perception and action. The challenge is to understand how hallmarks of higher cognition, productivity, systematicity, and compositionality, may emerge from such a bottom-up approach. To address this challenge, we present key ideas from Dynamic Field Theory which postulates that neural populations are organized by recurrent connectivity to create stable localist representations. Dynamic instabilities enable the autonomous generation of sequences of mental states. The capacity to apply neural circuitry across broad sets of inputs that emulates the function call postulated in symbolic computation emerges through coordinate transforms implemented in neural gain fields. We show how binding localist neural representations through a shared index dimension enables conceptual structure, in which the interdependence among components of a representation is flexibly expressed. We demonstrate these principles in a neural dynamic architecture that represents and perceptually grounds nested relational and action phrases. Sequences of neural processing steps are generated autonomously to attentionally select the referenced objects and events in a manner that is sensitive to their interdependencies. This solves the problem of 2 and the massive binding problem in expressions such as "the small tree that is to the left of the lake which is to the left of the large tree". We extend earlier work by incorporating new types of grammatical constructions and a larger vocabulary. We discuss the DFT framework relative to other neural process accounts of higher cognition and assess the scope and challenges of such neural theories.

papers.title: Dissecting Lottery Ticket Transformers: Structural and Behavioral Study of Sparse Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does iterative magnitude pruning affect the learned representations and internal structures of Transformers for neural machine translation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that iterative magnitude pruning degrades complex semantic knowledge first, causes higher layers to diverge and become less complex, shifts encoding burden to early layers, but leaves attention mechanisms largely unchanged.
papers.conclusion: The paper evaluates how unstructured pruning affects Transformer behavior while maintaining task performance, showing pruning degrades semantic knowledge before BLEU, early sparse layers better encode low-level information, representational changes occur in higher layers, and attention distributions remain similar.
papers.key_findings:
Complex semantic information is lost first during pruning, before BLEU decreases.
Model activations steadily diverge from unpruned representations, particularly at higher layers.
Information flow becomes more distributed in sparse Transformers: lower layers perform more encoding.
Attention mechanisms remain remarkably consistent across sparsities.
Encoder-decoder attention is the richest in representation, whereas decoder self-attention is the simplest.
papers.limitation:
BLEU is an imperfect measure of translation quality, so pruned models may perform worse than suggested.
The work focuses solely on magnitude pruning, which may not be representative of other pruning methods.
Probing classifiers measure correlation between model outputs and auxiliary information, not necessarily what information the model uses during its forward pass.
future_direction: Future work could analyze a model's encoded knowledge in other ways beyond probing.
Differences in how directly sparse and dense models encode information is an interesting question for future study, potentially using minimum description lengths.
papers.abstract: Recent work on the lottery ticket hypothesis has produced highly sparse Transformers for NMT while maintaining BLEU. However, it is unclear how such pruning techniques affect a model's learned representations. By probing Transformers with more and more lowmagnitude weights pruned away, we find that complex semantic information is first to be degraded. Analysis of internal activations reveals that higher layers diverge most over the course of pruning, gradually becoming less complex than their dense counterparts. Meanwhile, early layers of sparse models begin to perform more encoding. Attention mechanisms remain remarkably consistent as sparsity increases.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens. We show that this can be easily alleviated by removing residual connections in an encoder layer. With this modification, we gain up to 18.5 BLEU points on zero-shot translation while retaining quality on supervised directions. The improvements are particularly prominent between related languages, where our proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation. Moreover, our approach allows easy integration of new languages, which substantially expands translation coverage. By thorough inspections of the hidden layer outputs, we show that our approach indeed leads to more language-independent representations.

papers.title: Specialization after Generalization: Towards Understanding Test-Time Training in Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Why and when is test-time training (TTT) effective for foundation models, particularly for in-distribution data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that test-time training enables 'specialization after generalization,' allowing underparameterized foundation models to locally specialize on relevant concepts, which improves in-distribution performance.
papers.conclusion: Test-time training is an effective mechanism for specialization after generalization in foundation models, particularly when models are underparameterized and concepts are superimposed in the feature space.
papers.key_findings:
TTT improves predictions locally for underparameterized models by specializing the model to concepts relevant to the test task.
The performance gain from TTT diminishes as models become overparameterized and can globally disentangle more concepts.
Under the linear representation hypothesis, TTT can achieve a smaller in-distribution test error than global training when the feature space is exponentially smaller than the concept space.
Empirical scaling studies on image and language tasks confirm TTT is most effective in the underparameterized regime.
TTT implicitly finds sparse solutions in the underlying concept space, adjusting coefficients based on only a few relevant concepts.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis and key observations are made under the linear representation hypothesis.
future_direction: Exploring connections between TTT and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent empirical studies have explored the idea of continuing to train a model at test-time for a given task, known as test-time training (TTT), and have found it to yield significant performance improvements. However, there is limited understanding of why and when TTT is effective. Earlier explanations mostly focused on the observation that TTT may help when applied to out-of-distribution adaptation or used with privileged data. However, the growing scale of foundation models with most test data being in-distribution questions these explanations. We instead posit that foundation models remain globally underparameterized, with TTT providing a mechanism for specialization after generalization, focusing capacity on concepts relevant to the test task. Specifically, under the linear representation hypothesis, we propose a model in which TTT achieves a substantially smaller in-distribution test error than global training. We empirically validate our model's key assumptions by training a sparse autoencoder on ImageNet, showing that semantically related data points are explained by only a few shared concepts. Finally, we perform scaling studies across image and language tasks that confirm the practical implications of our model, identifying the regimes where specialization is most effective.

papers.title: On Efficient Transformer-Based Image Pre-training for Low-Level Vision
papers.research_question: How does pre-training act in image processing systems (low-level vision tasks) and what are effective pre-training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes how pre-training affects internal representations in low-level vision tasks and finds that multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than other strategies.
papers.conclusion: Pre-training plays a central role in developing stronger intermediate representations by incorporating more local information, and its effect is task-specific. Multi-related-task pre-training is highly effective and data-efficient for low-level vision.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-training introduces more local information to higher layers in super-resolution and deraining, yielding significant performance gains, while it hardly affects internal feature representations in denoising, resulting in limited gains.
Multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than single-task or multi-unrelated-task pre-training.
Larger model capacities generally obtain more improvements from pre-training.
Transformers benefit more from pre-training than CNNs, providing higher performance baselines with fewer parameters.
The internal representations of SR and deraining models show clear stages (more local in early layers, more global in higher layers), while denoising models present a relatively uniform structure filled with local information.
papers.limitation:
The study mainly investigates pre-training on synthesized data; future research should explore real-world settings and more tasks, extended to video processing.
The encoder-decoder design uses a fixed downsampling strategy, which may not be optimal for all degradation levels; adaptive downsampling could be better.
future_direction: Explore pre-training in real-world settings and more tasks.
Extend the study to video processing.
Investigate adaptive downsampling based on degradation degrees.
papers.abstract: Pre-training has marked numerous state of the arts in high-level computer vision, while few attempts have ever been made to investigate how pre-training acts in image processing systems. In this paper, we tailor transformer-based pre-training regimes that boost various low-level tasks. To comprehensively diagnose the influence of pre-training, we design a whole set of principled evaluation tools that uncover its effects on internal representations. The observations demonstrate that pre-training plays strikingly different roles in low-level tasks. For example, pre-training introduces more local information to higher layers in super-resolution (SR), yielding significant performance gains, while pre-training hardly affects internal feature representations in denoising, resulting in limited gains. Further, we explore different methods of pre-training, revealing that multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than other alternatives. Finally, we extend our study to varying data scales and model sizes, as well as comparisons between transformers and CNNs-based architectures. Based on the study, we successfully develop state-of-the-art models for multiple low-level tasks. Code is released at https://github.com/fenglinglwb/EDT.

papers.title: Exploring the Representation Manifolds of Stable Diffusion Through the Lens of Intrinsic Dimension
papers.research_question: How do prompts affect the intrinsic dimension of internal representations in Stable Diffusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that prompt choice significantly affects the intrinsic dimension of representations in Stable Diffusion, with correlation to prompt perplexity in bottleneck layers.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic dimension could be a useful tool for future studies of the impact of different prompts on text-to-image models.
papers.key_findings:
Prompts have a substantial effect on the intrinsic dimension of internal representations, with variations up to 10 dimensions.
Intrinsic dimension in latent representations decreases monotonically during denoising, while in bottleneck representations it forms a U-shaped curve.
In bottleneck layers, intrinsic dimension correlates with prompt perplexity, suggesting that less likely prompts result in higher-dimensional representations.
The dynamics of intrinsic dimension over denoising steps depend on the layer from which representations are extracted.
The time step embedding vector contributes to the increase in intrinsic dimension in bottleneck representations at later denoising steps.
papers.limitation: The correlation between perplexity and intrinsic dimension must be treated with caution, as it is not observed in latent representations.
future_direction: Adapting the experiments to other text-to-image models like DALL-E.
Comparing perplexity scores with actual frequencies of prompt tokens in training data like LAION-5B.
More comprehensive studies of other models that utilize prompts.
papers.abstract: Prompting has become an important mechanism by which users can more effectively interact with many flavors of foundation model. Indeed, the last several years have shown that well-honed prompts can sometimes unlock emergent capabilities within such models. While there has been a substantial amount of empirical exploration of prompting within the community, relatively few works have studied prompting at a mathematical level. In this work we aim to take a first step towards understanding basic geometric properties induced by prompts in Stable Diffusion, focusing on the intrinsic dimension of internal representations within the model. We find that choice of prompt has a substantial impact on the intrinsic dimension of representations at both layers of the model which we explored, but that the nature of this impact depends on the layer being considered. For example, in certain bottleneck layers of the model, intrinsic dimension of representations is correlated with prompt perplexity (measured using a surrogate model), while this correlation is not apparent in the latent layers. Our evidence suggests that intrinsic dimension could be a useful tool for future studies of the impact of different prompts on text-to-image models.

papers.title: Learning Hierarchically-Structured Concepts II: Overlapping Concepts, and Networks With Feedback
papers.research_question: How can hierarchically structured concepts with limited overlap be represented, recognized, and learned in neural networks that include feedback edges?
papers.core_contribution: Extends previous work by allowing limited overlap between concepts and feedback edges in networks, and provides algorithms for recognition and learning in these more general settings.
papers.conclusion: The paper extends the study of hierarchically structured concepts to allow overlap and feedback, providing recognition and learning algorithms with theoretical guarantees.
papers.key_findings:
For feed-forward networks, robust recognition algorithms are provided that work with approximate weights and scaling.
For networks with feedback, recognition algorithms require only two passes for tree hierarchies but may require more time for general hierarchies with overlap.
Learning algorithms for feed-forward networks are extended to handle overlap using a modified Winner-Take-All assumption.
Learning algorithms for networks with feedback use separate rules for upward and downward edges.
The learning behavior is reformulated in terms of achieving certain ranges of edge weights.
papers.limitation: The learning algorithms depend on Winner-Take-All subnetworks that are treated abstractly and not implemented.
future_direction: Studying recognition after partial learning.
Handling extraneous inputs and stochastic firing.
Implementing Winner-Take-All networks and interleaving learning of children and parents.
papers.abstract: We continue our study from Lynch and Mallmann-Trenn (Neural Networks, 2021), of how concepts that have hierarchical structure might be represented in brain-like neural networks, how these representations might be used to recognize the concepts, and how these representations might be learned. In Lynch and Mallmann-Trenn (Neural Networks, 2021), we considered simple tree-structured concepts and feed-forward layered networks. Here we extend the model in two ways: we allow limited overlap between children of different concepts, and we allow networks to include feedback edges. For these more general cases, we describe and analyze algorithms for recognition and algorithms for learning.

papers.title: Intriguing Equivalence Structures of the Embedding Space of Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: What are the algebraic and geometric structures of the embedding space of vision transformers, and how do they affect generalization and overgeneralization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that the embedding space of vision transformers consists of large piecewise linear subspaces where different inputs share the same representation and local normal spaces where visually indistinguishable inputs have very different representations, leading to overgeneralization and limited semantic generalization.
papers.conclusion: The embeddings produced by vision transformers are semantically limited due to the structure of their embedding space, which leads to overgeneralization and inherent vulnerability to adversarial attacks.
papers.key_findings:
The embedding space contains large piecewise linear subspaces where semantically different images can share the same representation.
There exist local normal spaces where visually indistinguishable images can have very different representations.
The model is highly sensitive to small input changes along certain directions (normal space) and invariant in others (null space).
The proposed gradient-based procedure can generate adversarial examples that alter an image's embedding to match a target, affecting downstream classification without model modification.
The findings are model-agnostic and dataset-agnostic, demonstrated across multiple vision transformer architectures and datasets.
future_direction: Formal exploration of the manifold structures of the embedding space
Application of the framework to other modalities
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large foundation models play a central role in the recent surge of artificial intelligence, resulting in fine-tuned models with remarkable abilities when measured on benchmark datasets, standard exams, and applications. Due to their inherent complexity, these models are not well understood. While small adversarial inputs to such models are well known, the structures of the representation space are not well characterized despite their fundamental importance. In this paper, using the vision transformers as an example due to the continuous nature of their input space, we show via analyses and systematic experiments that the representation space consists of large piecewise linear subspaces where there exist very different inputs sharing the same representations, and at the same time, local normal spaces where there are visually indistinguishable inputs having very different representations. The empirical results are further verified using the local directional estimations of the Lipschitz constants of the underlying models. Consequently, the resulting representations change the results of downstream models, and such models are subject to overgeneralization and with limited semantically meaningful generalization capability.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Reinforcement Learning Using Attention Augmented Agents
papers.research_question: How can an attention mechanism be used to create interpretable reinforcement learning agents while maintaining competitive performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a soft attention model for RL that provides interpretability through attention maps while achieving competitive performance on ATARI games.
papers.conclusion: The attention mechanism provides interpretability and competitive performance, and the agent learns meaningful attention strategies for decision making.
papers.key_findings:
The agent learns to attend to task-relevant objects like the player, enemies, and score.
The agent can react appropriately to novel, unseen configurations of the environment.
The agent performs forward planning/scanning by attending to possible future trajectories.
The agent uses 'trip wires' (attention at strategic points) to trigger specific actions.
The agent's queries separate 'what' (content) and 'where' (spatial) information.
papers.abstract: Inspired by recent work in attention models for image captioning and question answering, we present a soft attention model for the reinforcement learning domain. This model uses a soft, top-down attention mechanism to create a bottleneck in the agent, forcing it to focus on task-relevant information by sequentially querying its view of the environment. The output of the attention mechanism allows direct observation of the information used by the agent to select its actions, enabling easier interpretation of this model than of traditional models. We analyze different strategies that the agents learn and show that a handful of strategies arise repeatedly across different games. We also show that the model learns to query separately about space and content (`where' vs. `what'). We demonstrate that an agent using this mechanism can achieve performance competitive with state-of-the-art models on ATARI tasks while still being interpretable.

papers.title: Semantic Convergence: Investigating Shared Representations Across Scaled LLMs
papers.research_question: Do models with a fourfold difference in scale (Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B) converge on comparable internal concepts (feature universality)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that large language models of different sizes share aligned internal representations (feature universality), especially in middle layers, and that semantic subspaces and multi-token concepts are also similarly encoded.
papers.conclusion: The experiments reveal that internal representations are similar across models of different sizes, and that semantic subspaces and multi-token concepts are encoded similarly, reinforcing the concept of LLM universality.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B show the strongest overlap in feature representations, while early and late layers show less similarity.
Semantic subspaces (groups of related concepts) align across models, especially when the concepts are compatible (e.g., nature and people).
Multi-token subspaces are encoded similarly in early and middle layers, suggesting that models sometimes encode multi-token concepts rather than only single-token ones.
The alignment between models is statistically significant compared to random baselines, as measured by SVCCA and RSA.
Filtering out non-concept features (e.g., punctuation) makes the alignment patterns clearer and more meaningful.
papers.limitation:
The study focused only on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B due to resource constraints (GPU availability and compute time).
Using models with the same tokenizer leads to higher quality pairings and thus higher accuracy results.
The number of SAE-derived subspaces analyzed was limited to keep manual inspection and downstream evaluations manageable.
Experiments with multi-token subspaces only tested a single subspace due to resource limitations.
future_direction: Extend the approach to a wider range of architectures, parameter counts, tokenizers and layer comparisons.
Train SAEs on multiple model layers to reveal internal representations not captured in a single layer.
Compare the internal representations of SAEs trained on MLP layers to study universality of MLP features.
papers.abstract: We investigate feature universality in Gemma-2 language models (Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B), asking whether models with a four-fold difference in scale still converge on comparable internal concepts. Using the Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) dictionary-learning pipeline, we utilize SAEs on each model's residual-stream activations, align the resulting monosemantic features via activation correlation, and compare the matched feature spaces with SVCCA and RSA. Middle layers yield the strongest overlap, while early and late layers show far less similarity. Preliminary experiments extend the analysis from single tokens to multi-token subspaces, showing that semantically similar subspaces interact similarly with language models. These results strengthen the case that large language models carve the world into broadly similar, interpretable features despite size differences, reinforcing universality as a foundation for cross-model interpretability.

papers.title: What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models
papers.research_question: Does a foundation model's inductive bias align with a postulated world model, indicating that it has learned deeper structure from sequence prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an inductive bias probe to evaluate whether foundation models have learned a postulated world model, and finds that they often fail to do so, instead developing task-specific heuristics.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bias probe reveals that foundation models often fail to learn the underlying world models, instead relying on task-specific heuristics, which limits their generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models trained on orbital trajectories fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks.
Models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.
In lattice and Othello, models have an inductive bias toward legal next-tokens rather than the world model.
Models that perform better on inductive bias probes have better transfer performance on new tasks that rely on the underlying world model.
LLMs also fail to predict force magnitudes accurately in physics tasks.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning proprietary LLMs is infeasible and running the full inductive bias probe is expensive.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are premised on the idea that sequence prediction can uncover deeper domain understanding, much like how Kepler's predictions of planetary motion later led to the discovery of Newtonian mechanics. However, evaluating whether these models truly capture deeper structure remains a challenge. We develop a technique for evaluating foundation models that examines how they adapt to synthetic datasets generated from some postulated world model. Our technique measures whether the foundation model's inductive bias aligns with the world model, and so we refer to it as an inductive bias probe. Across multiple domains, we find that foundation models can excel at their training tasks yet fail to develop inductive biases towards the underlying world model when adapted to new tasks. We particularly find that foundation models trained on orbital trajectories consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis reveals that these models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: How are high-level human-interpretable features represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs, and how does the sparsity of these representations vary with model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse probing to localize individual neurons representing features in LLMs, revealing that early layers use superposition (sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons), middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons for higher-level features, and model scale increases representational sparsity with varied dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Sparse probing is a powerful tool for understanding feature representation in LLMs, revealing superposition in early layers and monosemantic neurons in middle layers, with scaling effects on sparsity, and opens many directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers represent many features in superposition via sparse linear combinations of polysemantic neurons.
Middle layers contain seemingly dedicated (monosemantic) neurons for higher-level contextual features like language or code.
Increasing model scale generally increases representational sparsity, but different features exhibit distinct scaling dynamics.
Sparse probing is an effective method for locating interpretable neurons, even when they are in superposition.
There is a tremendous amount of interpretable structure within the neurons of LLMs, accessible through careful probing and analysis.
papers.limitation:
Interpretation of neurons can be misleading due to 'interpretability illusions' from only examining maximum activating examples.
Conclusive statements about monosemanticity remain methodologically out of reach.
future_direction: Apply sparse probing to other model families and architectures.
Study the dynamics of feature representation during training, not just in final models.
Extend sparse probing to multimodal models and other modalities.
papers.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

papers.title: Bort: Towards Explainable Neural Networks with Bounded Orthogonal Constraint
papers.research_question: How can we improve the explainability of neural networks with mathematical guarantees via boundedness and orthogonality constraints on model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Bort, an optimizer with boundedness and orthogonality constraints that improves both explainability (comprehensibility and invertibility) and classification accuracy of various neural network architectures.
papers.conclusion: Bort improves both explainability and classification accuracy of neural networks by enforcing boundedness and orthogonality constraints, and enables feature decomposition and adversarial sample synthesis.
papers.key_findings:
Bort improves classification accuracy on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet for models like ResNet, VGG, DeiT, and Swin.
Bort enhances model explainability by improving reconstruction quality and saliency map precision.
Networks optimized by Bort allow for feature decomposition with sparse binarized variables, enabling adversarial sample synthesis without extra parameters or training.
The boundedness and orthogonality constraints are sufficient conditions for comprehensibility and invertibility, respectively.
Bort consistently outperforms baseline optimizers in both performance and explainability metrics.
papers.limitation: Bort is derived under the assumption of sufficiently wide networks; its properties for narrow or extremely deep networks are not investigated.
future_direction: Investigate the properties of Bort for narrow or extremely deep networks.
papers.abstract: Deep learning has revolutionized human society, yet the black-box nature of deep neural networks hinders further application to reliability-demanded industries. In the attempt to unpack them, many works observe or impact internal variables to improve the comprehensibility and invertibility of the black-box models. However, existing methods rely on intuitive assumptions and lack mathematical guarantees. To bridge this gap, we introduce Bort, an optimizer for improving model explainability with boundedness and orthogonality constraints on model parameters, derived from the sufficient conditions of model comprehensibility and invertibility. We perform reconstruction and backtracking on the model representations optimized by Bort and observe a clear improvement in model explainability. Based on Bort, we are able to synthesize explainable adversarial samples without additional parameters and training. Surprisingly, we find Bort constantly improves the classification accuracy of various architectures including ResNet and DeiT on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. Code: https://github.com/zbr17/Bort.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Exploring Compositionality in Vision Transformers using Wavelet Representations
papers.research_question: Does the Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder exhibit compositionality in its representations? Specifically, can the representation of an image be composed from the representations of its wavelet primitives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to test compositionality in ViT encoder representations using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) primitives and shows that ViT encoder representations are approximately compositional for one-level DWT decomposition.
papers.conclusion: ViT encoder representations exhibit compositional behavior when using primitives from a one-level DWT decomposition, providing a new perspective on how ViTs structure information.
papers.key_findings:
Simple summation of wavelet primitive representations does not reconstruct the original image's representation, indicating a lack of strict compositionality under addition.
A learnable linear composition function can approximate the original image's representation from the wavelet primitive representations, especially for one-level DWT decomposition.
The learned composition function assigns significantly higher weight to the low-pass (approximation) sub-band compared to detail sub-bands.
The proposed compositionality framework is robust to image distortions such as JPEG compression and additive Gaussian noise.
Compositionality is observed in the final encoder layer of ViT models (ViT-B and ViT-L) when using one-level DWT decomposition.
papers.limitation: The analysis is restricted to the final encoder layer of the ViT.
future_direction: Explore all encoder layers of the ViT for potential compositionality.
Explore other ways to study the error in composition.
papers.abstract: While insights into the workings of the transformer model have largely emerged by analysing their behaviour on language tasks, this work investigates the representations learnt by the Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder through the lens of compositionality. We introduce a framework, analogous to prior work on measuring compositionality in representation learning, to test for compositionality in the ViT encoder. Crucial to drawing this analogy is the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), which is a simple yet effective tool for obtaining input-dependent primitives in the vision setting. By examining the ability of composed representations to reproduce original image representations, we empirically test the extent to which compositionality is respected in the representation space. Our findings show that primitives from a one-level DWT decomposition produce encoder representations that approximately compose in latent space, offering a new perspective on how ViTs structure information.

papers.title: time2time: Causal Intervention in Hidden States to Simulate Rare Events in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do time series foundation models internalize semantic concepts like market regimes, and can their internal representations be leveraged to simulate rare events such as market crashes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation transplantation, a causal intervention method that provides evidence that time series foundation models learn high-level semantic concepts of real-world events, enabling steerable simulations for stress-testing.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides causal evidence that time series foundation models encode abstract, steerable market regime concepts, enabling deterministic control of forecasts and revealing a continuous severity axis in their latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Activation transplantation can deterministically steer forecasts by implanting the statistical signature of one event into another.
Models encode event severity as a continuous latent variable, with the activation vector norm correlating with shock magnitude.
The steerable representations are robust across different model architectures (decoder-only Toto and encoder-decoder Chronos).
A unified 'crash' concept emerges across layers, with early layers showing anti-correlation and later layers converging to a shared subspace.
The model's internal representation of a crash is not binary but continuous, allowing for graded interventions.
